techniques.name: Integrated Gradients
techniques.description: Integrated Gradients assigns input features scores for a prediction relative to a chosen reference input, called the baseline. It evaluates gradients, rates of output change, at points along a straight path from that reference to the actual input. Each feature's average gradient is multiplied by its change from the reference, and the resulting scores sum approximately to the output difference when enough numerical steps are used. For text, the path runs through continuous token representations rather than discrete word identifiers, and scores can be combined into highlighted words. In a protected-term variant, the reviewer fixes before the run a list of words or columns that name or record a protected characteristic, and reads the scores those inputs receive: a large score shows that the output rests partly on the characteristic, but a small score does not show that the model ignores it.

example_use_cases.description: An eye-screening programme evaluating a diabetic retinopathy grading model shows graders an Integrated Gradients heatmap beside each prediction, so they can see whether the regions driving a referral are lesions such as haemorrhages rather than camera artefacts, and uses the review to decide whether the model may assist grading.

A team building a question-answering assistant over an organisation's policy documents attributes each answer to the question's tokens and flags questions where the content words receive almost no attribution; those questions become test cases in which the content words are changed, to show whether the assistant actually reads the question.

A trust-and-safety team reviewing the posts its toxic-content classifier wrongly flagged fixes, before the run, a list of identity terms (names of religions, ethnicities and sexual orientations, chosen because the policy forbids penalising them) and computes Integrated Gradients against an all-padding baseline. Where a listed term ranks among the five most attributed tokens of a wrongly flagged post, the team adds counter-examples to the training data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A lender's model-risk team audits a classifier that reads the free-text statements in loan applications. Before the run it lists the words that state a protected characteristic, such as a religion, a pregnancy or a disability, and computes Integrated Gradients against a documented reference statement for a sample of declined applications. Any listed word among the ten most attributed is reported for a swap test; the absence of such words does not show the model ignores them.

limitations.description: Attributions are measured against the baseline and no choice is neutral. Features that match the baseline score near zero even when the model relies on them: with a black-image baseline, dark pixels on the object get little credit. A comparison of blurred, noise and training-data baselines found none best, so the baseline is an assumption to state and to vary before drawing conclusions.

Requires gradient access to a differentiable model, so it cannot explain tree ensembles, rule-based components or a model reached only through an API. For text, the path runs through token embeddings whose intermediate points are not real words, and subword tokenisation splits a word across several scores that must be recombined before a reviewer can read them.

Each explanation needs one gradient computation per step along the path; the original authors found 20 to 300 steps were usually enough for the scores to sum to within 5% of the output difference. Explaining long documents, high-resolution images or a large audit sample therefore costs tens to hundreds of forward and backward passes per prediction.

A score shows how sensitive the output was to a feature along one straight path, not that the feature causes the outcome in the world or that removing it would change the decision. Maps over neighbouring pixels or tokens are often noisy, and a plausible-looking heatmap does not show that the model's reasoning is sound.

resources.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
resources.abstract: We study the problem of attributing the prediction of a deep network to its input features, a problem previously studied by several other works. We identify two fundamental axioms---Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance that attribution methods ought to satisfy. We show that they are not satisfied by most known attribution methods, which we consider to be a fundamental weakness of those methods. We use the axioms to guide the design of a new attribution method called Integrated Gradients. Our method requires no modification to the original network and is extremely simple to implement; it just needs a few calls to the standard gradient operator. We apply this method to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model, demonstrating its ability to debug networks, to extract rules from a network, and to enable users to engage with models better.

Using a Deep Learning Algorithm and Integrated Gradients Explanation to Assist Grading for Diabetic Retinopathy
resources.abstract: PURPOSE: To understand the impact of deep learning diabetic retinopathy (DR) algorithms on physician readers in computer-assisted settings. DESIGN: Evaluation of diagnostic technology. PARTICIPANTS: One thousand seven hundred ninety-six retinal fundus images from 1612 diabetic patients. METHODS: Ten ophthalmologists (5 general ophthalmologists, 4 retina specialists, 1 retina fellow) read images for DR severity based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy disease severity scale in each of 3 conditions: unassisted, grades only, or grades plus heatmap. Grades-only assistance comprised a histogram of DR predictions (grades) from a trained deep-learning model. For grades plus heatmap, we additionally showed explanatory heatmaps. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: For each experiment arm, we computed sensitivity and specificity of each reader and the algorithm for different levels of DR severity against an adjudicated reference standard. We also measured accuracy (exact 5-class level agreement and Cohen's quadratically weighted κ), reader-reported confidence (5-point Likert scale), and grading time. RESULTS: Readers graded more accurately with model assistance than without for the grades-only condition (P < 0.001). Grades plus heatmaps improved accuracy for patients with DR (P < 0.001), but reduced accuracy for patients without DR (P = 0.006). Both forms of assistance increased readers' sensitivity moderate-or-worse DR: unassisted: mean, 79.4% [95% confidence interval (CI), 72.3%-86.5%]; grades only: mean, 87.5% [95% CI, 85.1%-89.9%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 88.7% [95% CI, 84.9%-92.5%] without a corresponding drop in specificity (unassisted: mean, 96.6% [95% CI, 95.9%-97.4%]; grades only: mean, 96.1% [95% CI, 95.5%-96.7%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 95.5% [95% CI, 94.8%-96.1%]). Algorithmic assistance increased the accuracy of retina specialists above that of the unassisted reader or model alone; and increased grading confidence and grading time across all readers. For most cases, grades plus heatmap was only as effective as grades only. Over the course of the experiment, grading time decreased across all conditions, although most sharply for grades plus heatmap. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning algorithms can improve the accuracy of, and confidence in, DR diagnosis in an assisted read setting. They also may increase grading time, although these effects may be ameliorated with experience.

techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

techniques.name: Taylor Decomposition
techniques.description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

example_use_cases.description: A quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defective printed circuit boards. For each flagged board they draw the deep Taylor heatmap and check that the highlighted pixels sit on the defect and not on a board label, the edge or the background, before they trust the flags enough to stop manual inspection.

A hospital's model-validation group audits a ReLU network that classifies chest X-rays. For a sample of positive cases, deep Taylor relevance shows whether the evidence for the finding lies inside the lungs or on markers, text or borders added by the imaging equipment, before the group signs the model off for a pilot.

A bank's data science team has a ReLU network that scores small-business loan applications from tabular inputs. For a declined application, deep Taylor relevance lists which inputs supplied most of the score, so a reviewer can see whether the decision rests on repayment history and income or on a field such as postcode.

limitations.description: The explanation depends on the choice of root point, and different reference inputs give different attributions. Finding the nearest root needs an iterative optimisation that is slow for large networks and may not converge, which is why the source applies the deep variant to large image networks.

Plain Taylor decomposition uses only first-order terms, so joint effects of several inputs stay unattributed and the scores need not add up to the prediction. In the source's tests the nearest-root version lost a large share of the relevance, so its heatmaps can leave much of the prediction unexplained.

The deep variant's guarantees, scores that add up to the prediction and are never negative, are proved for ReLU-style layers with zero or negative biases, and iNNvestigate documents support for ReLU networks only. Other activations, positive biases or normalisation layers need workarounds that the proofs do not cover.

Heatmaps explain one input at a time and are hard to validate. The source judges them by eye and by checking that relevance is conserved on MNIST digits and ImageNet photos, so a plausible-looking map does not prove that the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Requires access to internal layer operations and supported redistribution rules. A prediction-only service cannot supply this layer-wise decomposition, and an image-derived rule should not be assumed valid for arbitrary text or attention models.

resources.title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
resources.abstract: Nonlinear methods such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are the gold standard for various challenging machine learning problems, e.g., image classification, natural language processing or human action recognition. Although these methods perform impressively well, they have a significant disadvantage, the lack of transparency, limiting the interpretability of the solution and thus the scope of application in practice. Especially DNNs act as black boxes due to their multilayer nonlinear structure. In this paper we introduce a novel methodology for interpreting generic multilayer neural networks by decomposing the network classification decision into contributions of its input elements. Although our focus is on image classification, the method is applicable to a broad set of input data, learning tasks and network architectures. Our method is based on deep Taylor decomposition and efficiently utilizes the structure of the network by backpropagating the explanations from the output to the input layer. We evaluate the proposed method empirically on the MNIST and ILSVRC data sets.

techniques.name: Gradient Saliency
techniques.description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers, showing which pixels the score for a chosen class is most sensitive to. It takes the gradient of the class score (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital imaging team validating a pneumonia detection model on chest X-rays computes gradient saliency for a sample of confirmed cases and checks whether the most sensitive pixels lie over the lungs rather than over tubes, monitoring leads or position markers. They use the result to decide whether the model is ready for a clinical pilot or needs retraining on cleaner images.

An agricultural technology company testing a plant disease classifier on leaf photographs taken in the field computes gradient saliency for the images it misclassifies. It checks whether the sensitive pixels sit on the diseased leaf area or on soil, trays and hands in the frame, and decides whether to collect photographs with more varied backgrounds.

limitations.description: Maps are noisy and can change sharply for tiny changes to the image, so one map is weak evidence. A study of upper-limb X-ray classifiers found that plain-gradient maps were less accurate at locating abnormalities, and less repeatable, than radiologists' markings (Venkatesh et al., 2024). Look at many images and more than one trained model before drawing a conclusion about the model.

The gradient is local. Where the model's output has flattened, for example once a feature is already strongly present, the gradient is near zero, so a pixel the model relies on can get almost no score. Sundararajan et al. (2017) show this with a one-ReLU example, which is why methods such as Integrated Gradients measure the change from a baseline instead.

Because only the size of each gradient is kept, the map cannot say whether a pixel supports or counts against the chosen class. Evidence that argues against the prediction looks the same as evidence for it, so a map cannot show that a pixel was used in the way a reviewer assumes.

A high score means the output is sensitive to a small change in that pixel, not that the model relied on it or that removing it would change the decision. Pixel-level scores are scattered and often capture only the most discriminative part of an object (Simonyan et al., 2013), so they rarely outline a whole lesion or object a reviewer can name.

resources.title: Deep Inside Convolutional Networks: Visualising Image Classification Models and Saliency Maps
resources.abstract: This paper addresses the visualisation of image classification models, learnt using deep Convolutional Networks (ConvNets). We consider two visualisation techniques, based on computing the gradient of the class score with respect to the input image. The first one generates an image, which maximises the class score [Erhan et al., 2009], thus visualising the notion of the class, captured by a ConvNet. The second technique computes a class saliency map, specific to a given image and class. We show that such maps can be employed for weakly supervised object segmentation using classification ConvNets. Finally, we establish the connection between the gradient-based ConvNet visualisation methods and deconvolutional networks [Zeiler et al., 2013].

resources.title: Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

techniques.name: Influence Functions
techniques.description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction, so a reviewer can inspect the top few for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases. The theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, so for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting rather than proving why the model erred.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital analytics team finds that its readmission model misclassifies many children. For a misclassified child, influence functions single out a handful of paediatric training records with far more influence than any others, showing that the training data holds very few children. The team collects more paediatric data before deciding whether the model can be used on that group.

An email-security team asks why its spam filter blocked a legitimate supplier invoice. It lists the training emails with the most influence on that decision, finds near-duplicate phishing messages with a similar layout, and decides whether to relabel, remove or down-weight them before retraining the filter.

limitations.description: Exact influence needs the inverse of the Hessian, which is out of reach for networks with millions of parameters. Implementations approximate it with Hessian-vector products or block-diagonal and low-rank forms, which still costs extra passes over the training data for every prediction explained and adds error. Plan to explain a sample of decisions, not all of them.

Needs the full training set, the loss function and parameters at or near a minimum of the training loss. A model delivered as an API or a finished file, or trained on data the assessor cannot see, cannot be examined. For models that are early-stopped or not trained to a minimum, the paper adds a damping term to the Hessian, one more setting that can change the ranking.

The derivation assumes a convex, twice-differentiable loss. On a non-convex CNN the paper still found a 0.86 correlation with actual retraining, but a larger study found estimates often erroneous for deeper networks and dependent on architecture, weight decay and the test point (Basu et al., 2020). Check the estimates against real retraining on a few examples before relying on them.

Losses with kinks, such as the hinge loss of a support vector machine, break the method. In the paper, influence computed on the unsmoothed hinge loss considerably overestimated the effect of removal, and a smooth approximation of the loss was needed. Check that the loss is smooth for the model in hand, or smooth it for the calculation.

resources.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
resources.abstract: How can we explain the predictions of a black-box model? In this paper, we use influence functions — a classic technique from robust statistics — to trace a model's prediction through the learning algorithm and back to its training data, thereby identifying training points most responsible for a given prediction. To scale up influence functions to modern machine learning settings, we develop a simple, efficient implementation that requires only oracle access to gradients and Hessian-vector products. We show that even on non-convex and non-differentiable models where the theory breaks down, approximations to influence functions can still provide valuable information. On linear models and convolutional neural networks, we demonstrate that influence functions are useful for multiple purposes: understanding model behavior, debugging models, detecting dataset errors, and even creating visually-indistinguishable training-set attacks.

resources.title: Explaining Black Box Predictions and Unveiling Data Artifacts through Influence Functions
resources.abstract: Modern deep learning models for NLP are notoriously opaque.This has motivated the development of methods for interpreting such models, e.g., via gradient-based saliency maps or the visualization of attention weights.Such approaches aim to provide explanations for a particular model prediction by highlighting important words in the corresponding input text.While this might be useful for tasks where decisions are explicitly influenced by individual tokens in the input, we suspect that such highlighting is not always suitable for tasks where model decisions should be driven by more complex reasoning.In this work, we investigate the use of influence functions for NLP, providing an alternative approach to interpreting neural text classifiers.Influence functions explain the decisions of a model by identifying influential training examples.Despite the promise of this approach, influence functions have not yet been extensively evaluated in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work.We conduct a comparison between influence functions and common word-saliency methods on representative tasks.As suspected, we find that influence functions are particularly useful for natural language inference, a task in which 'saliency maps' may not provide clear interpretation.Furthermore, we develop a new quantitative measure based on influence functions that can reveal artifacts in training data.

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains model decisions by generating contrastive examples that reveal what makes a prediction distinctive. It identifies 'pertinent negatives' (minimal features that could be removed to change the prediction) and 'pertinent positives' (minimal features that must be present to maintain the prediction). This approach helps users understand not just what led to a decision, but what would need to change to achieve a different outcome, providing actionable insights for decision-making.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining loan application rejections by showing that removing recent late payments (pertinent negative) or adding £5,000 more annual income (pertinent positive) would change the decision to approval, giving applicants clear actionable guidance.

Analysing medical diagnosis models by identifying that removing a specific symptom combination would change a high-risk classification to low-risk, helping clinicians understand the critical diagnostic factors.

Providing transparent hiring decisions by showing job candidates exactly which qualifications (pertinent positives) they need to acquire or which application elements (pertinent negatives) might be hindering their success.

limitations.description: Computationally expensive as it requires solving an optimisation problem for each individual instance to find minimal perturbations.
Results can be highly sensitive to hyperparameter settings, requiring careful tuning to produce meaningful explanations.
May generate unrealistic or impossible contrastive examples if constraints are not properly specified, leading to impractical recommendations.
Limited to scenarios where feature perturbations are meaningful and actionable, making it less suitable for immutable characteristics or highly constrained domains.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

techniques.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
techniques.description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

resources.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
resources.abstract: Deep learning tools have gained tremendous attention in applied machine learning. However such tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty. In comparison, Bayesian models offer a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model uncertainty, but usually come with a prohibitive computational cost. In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs -- extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy. We perform an extensive study of the properties of dropout's uncertainty. Various network architectures and non-linearities are assessed on tasks of regression and classification, using MNIST as an example. We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.

Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

techniques.name: Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks
techniques.description: ODIN (Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks) flags inputs that look unlike the data a neural network classifier was trained on, and it works on an already trained network without retraining it. A classifier reports a confidence score, the highest probability it gives to any class, but that score is often high even for unfamiliar inputs. ODIN adjusts the score in two ways so that familiar and unfamiliar inputs separate better. It divides the classifier's raw output scores by a large constant, called the temperature, before turning them into probabilities, and it nudges the input slightly in the direction that raises the score, which lifts familiar inputs more than unfamiliar ones. An input whose adjusted score falls below a chosen threshold is flagged as out-of-distribution, so its prediction can be withheld or referred for review.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital screens each chest X-ray with ODIN before the diagnostic classifier's result is shown. Scans that are not chest X-rays, or that carry heavy artefacts, are flagged for human review instead of receiving a confident diagnosis, and the false positive rate is measured on a sample of such scans first.

An automated driving team scores each camera frame with ODIN and passes frames below the threshold to a fallback routine, such as slowing the vehicle and requesting remote assistance. The team measures how many unfamiliar frames, such as sensor faults or unusual scenes, are wrongly accepted before relying on the detector.

limitations.description: Temperature and perturbation size are tuned on a validation set that includes out-of-distribution examples, so some representative unfamiliar data is needed before deployment. The paper found settings transferred reasonably between validation sets, but only on image benchmarks.

Detection gets harder as unfamiliar inputs resemble the training data. In the original paper, at 95% acceptance of familiar images, the share of unfamiliar natural images wrongly accepted rose from at most about 11% with a 10-class training set to between 19% and 58% with a 100-class one, so performance must be measured on the deployment's own data.
Not designed to resist inputs deliberately crafted to look in-distribution, and the original paper does not evaluate adversarial evasion, so it gives no protection against a deliberate attacker.
Needs access to the network's gradients to compute the input perturbation, so it cannot be applied to a model that is reachable only through an API.
Each input needs at least one extra forward pass and one backward pass before the final scoring pass, which can matter for real-time or high-volume use.

resources.title: Enhancing The Reliability of Out-of-distribution Image Detection in Neural Networks
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of detecting out-of-distribution images in neural networks. We propose ODIN, a simple and effective method that does not require any change to a pre-trained neural network. Our method is based on the observation that using temperature scaling and adding small perturbations to the input can separate the softmax score distributions between in- and out-of-distribution images, allowing for more effective detection. We show in a series of experiments that ODIN is compatible with diverse network architectures and datasets. It consistently outperforms the baseline approach by a large margin, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance on this task. For example, ODIN reduces the false positive rate from the baseline 34.7% to 4.3% on the DenseNet (applied to CIFAR-10) when the true positive rate is 95%.

resources.title: Confidence-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Comparative Study and Analysis
resources.abstract: Image classification models deployed in the real world may receive inputs outside the intended data distribution. For critical applications such as clinical decision making, it is important that a model can detect such out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and express its uncertainty. In this work, we assess the capability of various state-of-the-art approaches for confidence-based OOD detection through a comparative study and in-depth analysis. First, we leverage a computer vision benchmark to reproduce and compare multiple OOD detection methods. We then evaluate their capabilities on the challenging task of disease classification using chest X-rays. Our study shows that high performance in a computer vision task does not directly translate to accuracy in a medical imaging task. We analyse factors that affect performance of the methods between the two tasks. Our results provide useful insights for developing the next generation of OOD detection methods.

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing reduces bias by training models using a competitive adversarial setup, similar to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The technique involves two neural networks: a predictor that learns to make accurate predictions on the main task, and an adversary (bias detector) that attempts to predict protected attributes (such as race, gender, or age) from the predictor's internal representations. Through adversarial training, the predictor learns to produce representations that retain predictive power for the main task whilst being uninformative about protected characteristics, thereby reducing discriminatory bias.

example_use_cases.description: Training a resume screening model for a technology company that evaluates candidates based on skills and experience whilst preventing the internal representations from encoding gender or ethnicity information, ensuring hiring decisions cannot be influenced by protected characteristics even indirectly through correlated features.

Developing a credit scoring model for loan approvals that accurately predicts default risk whilst ensuring the model's internal features cannot be used to infer applicants' race or age, thereby preventing discriminatory lending practices whilst maintaining predictive accuracy.

Creating a medical diagnosis model that makes accurate predictions about patient conditions whilst ensuring that the learned representations cannot reveal sensitive demographic information like gender or ethnicity, protecting patient privacy whilst maintaining clinical effectiveness.

limitations.description: Significantly more complex to implement than standard models, requiring expertise in adversarial training techniques and careful architecture design for both predictor and adversary networks.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the competing objectives of task performance and bias mitigation, as overly strong adversarial training can harm predictive accuracy.

Effectiveness heavily depends on the quality and design of the adversary network - a weak adversary may fail to detect subtle biases, whilst an overly strong adversary may eliminate useful information.
Training can be unstable and may suffer from convergence issues common to adversarial training, requiring careful learning rate scheduling and regularisation techniques.
Provides no formal guarantees about bias elimination and may not prevent all forms of discrimination, particularly when protected attributes can be inferred from other available features.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.
